card_summary: The growing adoption of AV1 is a clear indication that broadcast engineers will need to reassess their encoding and decoding strategies. With 40% of respondents planning to deploy AV1 in 2026, it's likely that we'll see a shift towards more flexible and scalable encoding architectures that can accommodate multiple codecs. This, in turn, will require a re-evaluation of the transport protocols used to move signals over IP networks, with ST 2110 and NMOS likely to play a key role in managing the increased complexity. In practice, this means that engineering teams will need to carefully manage latency and signal integrity as they transition to AV1. With H.264/AVC still dominating the market at 84% adoption, there's a risk of introducing additional latency and jitter as engineers work to integrate AV1 into their existing workflows. To mitigate this, teams should focus on implementing robust genlock and synchronization strategies, using tools like JPEG XS and SRT to ensure frame-accuracy and minimize latency.
body_html:
Why Broadcasters Must Rethink Signal Transport for AV1 Adoption

As the broadcast industry gears up for widespread adoption of AV1, the pressure is mounting on engineers to rethink their signal transport architectures. With 40% of respondents planning to deploy AV1 in 2026, the stakes are high for those who fail to adapt. The writing is on the wall: AV1's superior compression efficiency and lower latency will soon render older codecs obsolete.

What This Development Actually Means

The recent survey by Streaming Media Blog reveals that 84% of respondents already use H.264/AVC, but a significant 40% plan to deploy AV1 in the coming year. This seismic shift in codec adoption is driven by the need for better compression efficiency, lower latency, and improved quality.

This development is not an isolated incident; it's a symptom of a broader industry trend. The shift towards IP-based signal transport, driven by the adoption of ST 2110 and NMOS, has created an environment where new codecs like AV1 can thrive. The industry is moving away from traditional satellite and fibre-based transmission methods, which are often expensive and inflexible.

Why It Matters for Broadcast Operations

The adoption of AV1 will have significant implications for broadcast operations, particularly in terms of signal transport and latency. Engineers will need to reassess their infrastructure decisions, taking into account the increased complexity and integration requirements of AV1. For example, Harmonic's VOS360 encoding platform, which supports AV1, will require careful integration with existing ST 2110 and NMOS systems. Similarly, Telestream's Vantage platform, which also supports AV1, will need to be configured to work seamlessly with existing IP gateways like Matrox ConvertIP and Riedel MediorNet.

Impact by Stakeholder

  • Regional and national broadcasters: Will need to budget for new encoding and decoding hardware, as well as updated IP gateways and signal transport infrastructure. This will require significant CapEx investments, but will ultimately lead to reduced transmission costs and lower latency.
  • OTT and streaming platforms: Will need to update their ABR ladders and content delivery networks (CDNs) to support AV1. This will require careful planning and testing to ensure seamless integration with existing HLS and DASH delivery systems.
  • Post-production and MAM teams: Will need to update their ingest and QC workflows to accommodate AV1, which will require careful configuration of MAM systems like Avid iNEWS and Vizrt Trio.

Analysis: I've seen many CTOs excited about the prospect of deploying AV1, but they often overlook the fact that widespread adoption will require significant updates to their Content Delivery Networks (CDNs). Unless they're prepared to upgrade their CDNs to handle the increased overhead of AV1 encoding, they'll be stuck with inefficient content delivery, which could negate the benefits of the new codec.
